title: Present simple and present continuous for the future

sections.title: Present simple for fixed future events
sections.content:
Present simple
We can often use either the present simple or will to talk about future events that are part of some timetabled or programmed arrangement or routine. However, we prefer the present simple for fixed, unchangeable events. Compare:
• Does the sale finish on Thursday or Friday? (or Will the sale finish …?) and
• The sun rises at 5:16 tomorrow. (more likely than The sun will rise …)
We avoid the present simple when we talk about less formal or less routine arrangements, or predictions. Instead we use will, be going to, or the present continuous:
• Are you staying in to watch TV tonight, or are you coming dancing? (not Do you stay to watch TV tonight, or do you come…)
• It's only a problem in Britain now, but it will affect the rest of Europe soon. (not … but it affects the rest of Europe soon.)

sections.title: Present simple in time and conditional clauses
sections.content:
We use the present simple, not will, to refer to the future –
☆ in time clauses with conjunctions such as after, as soon as, before, by the time, when, while, until:
• When you see Ben, tell him he still owes me some money. (not When you will see Ben …)
• I should be finished by the time you get back. (not … by the time you will get back.)
☆ in real conditional clauses with if, in case, provided, and unless:
• Provided the right software is available, I should be able to solve the problem.
• I'll bring some sandwiches in case we don't find anywhere decent to eat.
☆ when we talk about possible future events with suppose, supposing, and what if:
• Suppose we miss the bus – how will we get home? (or Suppose we missed …)
• What if the train's late? Where shall I meet you then? (or What if the train was late?)

sections.title: Present continuous for planned future events
sections.content:
Present continuous
We can often use either the present continuous or be going to with a similar meaning to talk about planned future events. The present continuous indicates a firm intention or definite decision, though it may not already be arranged:
• Are you seeing the doctor again next week? (or Are you going to see …?)
• I'm not asking Tom to the party. (or I'm not going to ask …)
However, we don't use the present continuous for the future –
☆ when we make or report predictions about activities or events over which we have no control:
• I think it's going to rain soon.
• Scientists say that the satellite won't cause any damage when it falls to Earth.
☆ when we talk about permanent future situations:
• People are going to live / will live longer in the future.

sections.title: Avoiding be going to + go/come
sections.content:
Many people avoid be going to + go / come and use the present continuous forms instead:
• I'm going to town on Saturday. (rather than I'm going to go to town …)
• Are you coming home for lunch? (rather than Are you going to come …?)

exercises.question: We ___ our exam results on the 20th August.
exercises.hint: Not a fixed timetable — use will (uncertain/expected result).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will get
Use will rather than the present simple because this is not a fixed, institutionally scheduled event. Present simple is reserved for timetables and programmes (trains, shows, official fixtures). Anticipated or expected dates — like exam results or drug launches — take will.

exercises.question: Alex ___ our cats while we're away next week.
exercises.hint: Personal arrangement, not a programmed fixture — use will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will look after
Use will rather than the present simple because this is not a fixed, institutionally scheduled event. Present simple is reserved for timetables and programmes (trains, shows, official fixtures). Anticipated or expected dates — like exam results or drug launches — take will.

exercises.question: I think I'll take an umbrella in case it ___.
exercises.hint: In case + conditional clause → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: rains
After 'in case', 'when', 'before', 'after', 'until', and other time/conditional conjunctions, use the present simple to refer to future events. Do not use 'will' in these subordinate clauses.

exercises.question: There is a reading list to accompany my lecture, which I ___ at the end.
exercises.hint: Not a fixed timetable — use will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will read
Use will rather than the present simple because this is not a fixed, institutionally scheduled event. Present simple is reserved for timetables and programmes (trains, shows, official fixtures). Anticipated or expected dates — like exam results or drug launches — take will.

exercises.question: The new drug ___ on sale in the USA next year.
exercises.hint: Not a fixed programme — use will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will start
Use will rather than the present simple because this is not a fixed, institutionally scheduled event. Present simple is reserved for timetables and programmes (trains, shows, official fixtures). Anticipated or expected dates — like exam results or drug launches — take will.

exercises.question: The last train to Edinburgh ___ (leave) at 23:45.
exercises.hint: Fixed timetable event → present simple for scheduled future.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: leaves
Use the present simple for scheduled, timetabled events (transport, cinema, programmes). These are fixed in advance and do not depend on personal intention.

exercises.question: The concert ___ at 7:30, not 7:15 as it says in the programme.
exercises.hint: Fixed, programmed, unchangeable event → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: plays
Fixed, programmed, unchangeable event → present simple.

exercises.question: Provided it ___ raining, we'll go for a walk this afternoon.
exercises.hint: Provided (conditional clause) → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: stops
Provided (conditional clause) → present simple.

exercises.question: What if I ___ my plans and decide to stay longer?
exercises.hint: What if (hypothetical future clause) → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: change
What if (hypothetical future clause) → present simple.

exercises.question: We ___ Mariam when she leaves, but she says she'll keep in touch.
exercises.hint: Prediction (can't arrange missing someone) → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will miss
Use will for feelings about the future — predictions about emotions or states. These cannot be "arranged" like appointments, so the present continuous is not used. Will miss expresses a natural prediction about a future emotional state.

exercises.question: Unless my parents ___ me some money, I won't be able to go on holiday this year.
exercises.hint: Unless (conditional clause) → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: lend
In conditional clauses with 'unless', 'if', 'when', 'before', 'after', and 'until', use the present simple to refer to future events. The future tense ('will') belongs in the main clause, not the subordinate clause.

exercises.question: I ___ (meet) the director tomorrow at 10am. It's in my diary.
exercises.hint: Personal arrangement in the diary → present continuous for future.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: am meeting
Use the present continuous for personal arrangements and appointments — things that have been organised in advance between people. 'It's in my diary' confirms it's a personal plan.

exercises.question: Tonight France ___ Germany in a match important for both teams.
exercises.hint: Fixed scheduled sporting fixture → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: gives out
Fixed scheduled sporting fixture → present simple.

exercises.question: It is unlikely that the government ___ the court's decision.
exercises.hint: Prediction ('it is unlikely') → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will accept
After evaluative phrases like it is unlikely that, I doubt, or it is probable that, use will in the following clause. These phrases introduce future predictions framed by the speaker's assessment.

exercises.question: Supposing I ___ to upload a video to YouTube? How do I do that?
exercises.hint: Supposing (hypothetical future) → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: want
Supposing (hypothetical future) → present simple.

exercises.question: By the time you ___ this letter, I should be in New Zealand.
exercises.hint: By the time (time clause) → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: get
'By the time' introduces a time clause and is followed by the present simple for future reference. The main clause typically uses the future perfect ('will have + past participle') to show completion before that point.

exercises.question: It's not a deep cut, but it ___ a scar. (Which is WRONG?)
options: is leaving ✗ (wrong — can't arrange a scar)
exercises.hint: You can't arrange or control forming a scar → present continuous is wrong.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is leaving ✗ (wrong — can't arrange a scar)
You can't arrange or control forming a scar → present continuous is wrong. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: The exhibition ___ on the 15th — please arrive on time.
exercises.hint: Fixed, scheduled institutional event → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: opens
Scheduled institutional events (exhibitions, shows, performances) use the present simple to refer to the future. The date is fixed on a timetable — this is the same pattern as 'The train leaves at 9am'.

exercises.question: Did you know I ___ a new car next week? (Which is WRONG?)
exercises.hint: An arranged plan — will suggests an impulsive decision, which seems unlikely here.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will buy ✗ (unlikely — it's arranged)
After evaluative phrases like it is unlikely that, I doubt, or it is probable that, use will in the following clause. These phrases introduce future predictions framed by the speaker's assessment.

exercises.question: A: We can take you. We ___ you up at eight. (Which is WRONG?)
exercises.hint: No prior arrangement — present continuous implies it's already fixed, which it isn't.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are picking ✗ (not yet arranged)
The present continuous is used for fixed personal arrangements — plans agreed and settled in advance with other people, typically recorded in a diary. The arrangement exists now as a present fact, even though the event is in the future.

exercises.question: I'm sorry I can't come for dinner. I ___ to York tonight. (Which is WRONG?)
exercises.hint: An arranged plan to go to York → will is unlikely here.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will drive ✗ (unlikely — it's arranged)
After evaluative phrases like it is unlikely that, I doubt, or it is probable that, use will in the following clause. These phrases introduce future predictions framed by the speaker's assessment.

exercises.question: The high-speed rail link ___ the journey time significantly. (Which is WRONG?)
exercises.hint: Can't arrange a rail link cutting journey time → present continuous is wrong.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is cutting ✗ (not an arranged event)
Can't arrange a rail link cutting journey time → present continuous is wrong. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: I have to go now. I ___ you back later today. (Which is WRONG?)
options: am going to call ✗ (implies prior plan)
exercises.hint: Calling back is a spontaneous promise at the moment of speaking → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: am calling ✗ (not arranged)
The present continuous describes a temporary action or situation in progress around the present moment. The key signals here are words like at the moment, today, currently, or right now. Compare with the present simple, which describes permanent facts or habitual actions.

exercises.question: The exhibition runs from the 15th and ___ on the 30th.
exercises.hint: Fixed schedule end date → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: closes
Both the opening and closing of the exhibition are fixed on an institutional timetable. Use the present simple for future events that are scheduled and will not change: opens, closes, starts, ends, departs, arrives.

exercises.question: Don't go out now. I ___ lunch in a moment. (Which is WRONG?)
exercises.hint: Serving is about to happen — present continuous or be going to, not will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will serve ✗
Serving is about to happen — present continuous or be going to, not will. Use will here — this is neither a fixed timetable event (which would take the present simple) nor a pre-planned personal arrangement (which would take the present continuous or be going to).

exercises.question: Unless help arrives within the next few days, thousands ___. (Which is WRONG?)
exercises.hint: Prediction of uncontrolled future event → present continuous is wrong.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are starving ✗ (can't arrange starvation)
Prediction of uncontrolled future event → present continuous is wrong. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: Simon Bianchi ___ us for dinner, the novelist.
exercises.hint: Previously arranged plan → be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is going to join
Previously arranged plan → be going to. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: I'm sure you ___ him.
exercises.hint: Prediction based on opinion → will.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will like
Use will for general predictions based on opinion, knowledge, or experience — not on present visible evidence. When there is present physical evidence (dark clouds, someone is about to fall), use be going to instead.

exercises.question: His latest book ___ (come) out at the end of this week.
exercises.hint: Firm arrangement/schedule → present continuous.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is coming
The present continuous is used for fixed personal arrangements — plans agreed and settled in advance with other people, typically recorded in a diary. The arrangement exists now as a present fact, even though the event is in the future.

exercises.question: Have you heard that BWM ___ 300 workers?
exercises.hint: Known plan/prior decision → be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is going to sack
Known plan/prior decision → be going to. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.

exercises.question: Supposing they ___ completely — that would be awful.
exercises.hint: Supposing + hypothetical future clause → present simple.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: close
Supposing + hypothetical future clause → present simple.

exercises.question: I've heard that they ___ a new factory in Ireland.
exercises.hint: Known prior plan → be going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: are going to build
Known prior plan → be going to. The present continuous shows that the action is temporary or in progress now. Look for context signals: at the moment, currently, today, or a sense of ongoing change or temporary situation.
